chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
title: Giving Bechet a job at the Circle Ballroom
summary: Bechet could not get a cabaret card, so Moore hired him in his band at a taxi-dance hall, where Bechet could not read stocks.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend

blocks.x: I see. Now, Bechet. Had you met Bechet before? Say, before you even worked with Kirby?
Yeah. I met Bechet... I was working someplace... I think in the spare time I had... I was talking a few minutes ago about I had about a few weeks off or something...
I was down in a place called...58th Street and Eighth Avenue, one flight upstairs, a dance hall, a taxi

dance hall. I forgot the name of the place, the hall... Whatever I did down there... Pretty good job... Taxi-dance hall. I think I had a five-piece band down there. And Sidney Bechet... During that time, Sidney Bechet wasn't doing nothing. The whole thing about it is, he got in a little trouble, and he couldn't get no cabaret card, and he couldn't work no place around here. So I was thinking about it. I was thinking about Sidney getting no cabaret, and I gave him a job. You know, I had a job for him with my band... Circle Ballroom.

Yeah. At 58th Street and Eighth Avenue, one flight upstairs. That's a long ways (?). What year was that I can't remember. But anyway, I was getting thirty dollars a week; I was the leader of the band. The scale around about that time was about twenty or twenty-five dollars. Bechet worked with me a long time. And the boss gave me five dollars extra, so I was getting thirty dollars -- which everybody was getting twenty-five. He gave me five dollars more to buy music. I had to bring in some music every night, every two nights. During that time the stocks... I mean, you used a lot of stocks. The stocks were twenty or fifteen...fifteen cents a stock, some of them twenty cents, some twenty-five cents, some thirty-five
cents. And we'd play all those stocks.
They were cheap in that time.

And Bechet, it was (?), he couldn't read the stocks. He could play all right, but he just couldn't read them stocks. He never wanted to know it. That's the way it is. So I had to get somebody to read the stocks. So I got hold of a fellow named Happy Caldwell, a tenor player. He'd been at (?) for a while. But I was down there, I guess, about three or four years, I think, or something...
